questions.question: What are the differences between Monolithic, Microservices, and Modular Monolith architectures?
questions.title: Monolith vs Microservices vs Modular Monolith
questions.direct_answer: **Monolith** = one deployable, one codebase, one DB — simplest to build and operate, but all teams share a release pipeline and a single failure domain. **Microservices** = many small independently deployable services, each with its own DB, communicating over the network — enables team autonomy and independent scaling, at the cost of distributed-system complexity (networking, eventual consistency, observability). **Modular Monolith** = single deployable but with **strict module boundaries** internally (each module owns its data, exposes a contract) — you get most of microservices' design discipline without the operational tax. **Default to a modular monolith**; extract services only when team size, scaling, or deployment cadence forces the issue.

interviewer_intent.testing: Trade-offs of each (not just 'microservices = good'), why modular monolith is often the right starting point, and the criteria for extracting a service.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating microservices as universally better, or thinking 'microservices = small'. Size isn't the point — deployment independence is.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss the operational tax of microservices (CI/CD, observability, on-call, data consistency), and walk through the modular monolith → selective extraction migration path.

sections.title: The Three Models
sections.content:
**Monolith:**
- Single deployable artifact (one JAR/WAR), one DB.
- One CI/CD pipeline, one team can know it all.
- Internal calls are method calls (fast, transactional, type-checked).
- All teams release together.

**Microservices:**
- Many small services, each independently deployable, each with its own DB.
- Communication over network (REST, gRPC, async events).
- Each team owns one or more services end-to-end (you build it, you run it).
- Failures are partial; consistency is eventual.

**Modular Monolith:**
- Single deployable, but internally split into well-bounded modules (Maven modules, Gradle subprojects, packages with strict access rules).
- Each module owns its data (its own schema/tables); other modules call only via the module's public API.
- All deployed together, but designed as if extractable.
- One pipeline, one DB instance (with logical separation), but teams have clear ownership.

schemas per module)] D1 -.public API.-> D2 D2 -.public API.-> D3 D2 -.public API.-> D4 D1 --> DDB D2 --> DDB D3 --> DDB D4 --> DDB end subgraph Micro[Microservices] S1[Users svc] S2[Orders svc] S3[Payments svc] S4[Inventory svc] DB1[(Users DB)] DB2[(Orders DB)] DB3[(Payments DB)] DB4[(Inventory DB)] S1 -.HTTP/Kafka.-> S2 S2 -.HTTP/Kafka.-> S3 S2 -.HTTP/Kafka.-> S4 S1 --> DB1 S2 --> DB2 S3 --> DB3 S4 --> DB4 end ```

sections.title: Trade-Off Matrix
sections.content:
| Aspect | Monolith | Modular Monolith | Microservices |
|---|---|---|---|
| Deployable units | 1 | 1 | N |
| Database | 1 shared | 1 (logically separated) | N (one per service) |
| Internal calls | method | method (via module API) | network (HTTP/gRPC/async) |
| Transactions | local ACID | local ACID | distributed (Saga) |
| Team autonomy | low | medium | high |
| Independent scaling | no | no (process-level) | yes |
| Failure isolation | no | no | yes (partial failure) |
| Operational complexity | low | low | high |
| Observability | logs + APM | logs + APM | distributed tracing required |
| CI/CD | one pipeline | one pipeline | N pipelines + dependency graph |
| Onboarding cost | low | medium | high |
| Refactoring across boundaries | trivial | trivial | painful (cross-service) |
| Best for team size | 1-15 | 5-50 | 50+ across multiple teams |

sections.title: When Each Wins
sections.content:
**Monolith wins when:**
- Single small team (1-10 devs).
- Early-stage product; requirements churning weekly.
- Domain not yet understood enough to draw service boundaries.
- Strict consistency requirements (financial flows benefit from local ACID).

**Modular monolith wins when:**
- Team is growing (10-50) but still ships from one repo.
- Want microservices' design discipline without operational tax.
- Future-proofing: bounded modules can be extracted later when needed.
- DDD bounded contexts are clear, but cross-context performance matters (in-process calls).

**Microservices win when:**
- Multiple teams (50+) need independent release cadences.
- Different parts have wildly different scaling needs (search vs checkout).
- Different parts have different language/runtime needs (ML in Python, payments in Java).
- High-availability requirements need failure isolation (one service crash doesn't down everything).
- Independent data store requirements (analytics in OLAP store, search in Elasticsearch).

sections.title: The Hidden Cost of Microservices
sections.content:
Microservices aren't free. Real costs:

**Operations:**
- N CI/CD pipelines, N deployment strategies.
- Service discovery, config management, secret management.
- Distributed tracing required (without it, debugging is impossible).
- Centralized log aggregation.
- Service mesh or extensive client libraries.

**Data:**
- No cross-service joins; build read models / data projections.
- Distributed transactions → sagas + compensations.
- Event-driven architecture for consistency.
- Schema evolution coordinated across services.

**Networking:**
- Latency budget consumed by inter-service calls (each hop = 1-5ms).
- Retries, timeouts, circuit breakers everywhere.
- Backpressure and rate limiting.

**Team:**
- 24/7 on-call per service.
- Steeper hiring bar (every dev needs distributed-systems intuition).
- Cross-team dependencies hard to coordinate.

**Rule of thumb:** if 5 small teams could deliver the same product, microservices probably aren't worth it yet.

sections.title: Modular Monolith — The Pragmatic Default
sections.content:
**What it looks like in Java:**

```
order-service/
  pom.xml                    -- aggregator
  modules/
    users/
      pom.xml
      src/main/java/com/example/users/
        api/         -- public API (interfaces, DTOs)
        domain/      -- internal
        infra/       -- internal
    orders/
      api/, domain/, infra/
    payments/
      api/, domain/, infra/
```

**Rules enforced:**
- `orders` module declares only `users:api` as a Maven dependency — not `users:domain`.
- Tools like ArchUnit / jMolecules / Spring Modulith enforce that no class outside `users.api` is reachable from outside the `users` module.
- Each module owns its DB schema (`users.*`, `orders.*`).
- No cross-schema FKs; relationships modeled by ID reference and module API calls.

**Spring Modulith** makes this first-class: detects module boundaries, generates docs, supports event publication for module-to-module async (decoupled like microservices but in-process).

**Migration to microservices later:** because modules already speak through APIs and own their schemas, extraction is mostly: replace API calls with HTTP, move schema to a separate DB. Painful but tractable — not the rewrite a tangled monolith would be.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **'Microservices because Netflix did it.'** Netflix has 1000+ engineers and unique scale needs. Most companies don't.
- **Splitting too early.** Without understanding the domain, you'll draw boundaries wrong; refactoring across services is much harder than within one codebase.
- **Distributed monolith.** Microservices that can't deploy independently, that share a DB, or that always need to be released together — you have all the operational tax with none of the autonomy benefit.
- **Treating microservices as 'small'.** Tiny services (15-line nano-services) explode network calls; size should match a bounded context, not a function.
- **Ignoring the modular monolith middle ground.** Many teams jump from monolith straight to microservices and regret it.
- **No observability before going micro.** Without distributed tracing, debugging a 30-service system is nearly impossible.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Monolith:** one deployable, simple, low ops cost. Best for small teams.
- **Modular monolith:** single deployable with strict internal module boundaries; design discipline of microservices without the operational tax.
- **Microservices:** N independently deployable services, each with its own DB; team autonomy + independent scaling but high operational cost.
- **Trade-offs are real:** observability, distributed transactions, latency, on-call, CI/CD complexity.
- **Default to modular monolith;** extract services only when forced (team size, scaling, deployment cadence).
- **Spring Modulith** enables modular monolith first-class.
- **'Distributed monolith'** is the worst of both worlds — avoid.
- **Boundaries should follow business / DDD, not 'small functions'.**

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**The three models**

Monolith: single deployable, one codebase, one DB. Internal calls are method calls — fast, transactional, type-checked. All teams release together.

Microservices: many small services, each independently deployable, each with its own DB. Communication over network — REST, gRPC, async events. Each team owns end-to-end. Failures partial; consistency eventual.

Modular monolith: single deployable but internally split into well-bounded modules. Each owns its data, exposes a contract. Deployed together but designed as if extractable. One pipeline, one DB instance with logical separation.

**Trade-off matrix highlights**

Deployable units: 1 / 1 / N
Database: 1 shared / 1 logically separated / N per service
Internal calls: method / module API / network
Transactions: local ACID / local ACID / distributed via saga
Team autonomy: low / medium / high
Independent scaling: no / no / yes
Failure isolation: no / no / yes
Operational complexity: low / low / high
Observability: logs + APM / logs + APM / distributed tracing required

**When each wins**

Monolith: 1-10 devs, early-stage product, churning requirements, strict local-ACID needs.

Modular monolith: 10-50 team, want microservices discipline without operational tax, future-proofing for selective extraction, DDD bounded contexts clear but in-process performance matters.

Microservices: 50+ across multiple teams needing independent release cadences, wildly different scaling needs (search vs checkout), different runtimes (Python ML + Java payments), high-availability requires failure isolation, independent data store requirements.

**The hidden cost of microservices**

- Operations: N pipelines, service discovery, distributed tracing required, centralized logs, service mesh
- Data: no cross-service joins, sagas + compensations, event-driven for consistency, coordinated schema evolution
- Networking: latency budget consumed by hops, retries/timeouts/circuit breakers everywhere
- Team: 24/7 on-call per service, steeper hiring bar, cross-team coordination

Rule of thumb: if 5 small teams could deliver the same product, microservices probably aren't worth it yet.

**Modular monolith — the pragmatic default**

In Java: Maven aggregator with submodules. Each module exposes api/ (public), domain/ + infra/ (internal). Orders module depends only on users:api, not users:domain.

ArchUnit / jMolecules / Spring Modulith enforces no class outside users.api is reachable from outside the users module.

Each module owns its DB schema. No cross-schema FKs; relationships by ID reference and module API calls.

Spring Modulith makes this first-class: boundary detection, docs, event publication for module-to-module async (decoupled like microservices but in-process).

Migration to microservices later: because modules already speak through APIs and own schemas, extraction is replace API calls with HTTP + move schema to separate DB. Tractable, not a rewrite.

**Common mistakes**

- Microservices because Netflix did it — most companies aren't Netflix
- Splitting too early — wrong boundaries, harder to refactor across services
- Distributed monolith — services that can't deploy independently, share DB, always release together. Worst of both worlds
- Treating microservices as 'small' — nano-services explode network calls; size should match bounded context
- Ignoring modular monolith middle ground
- No observability before going micro — debugging 30 services without tracing is impossible

**Recommendation**

**Default to a modular monolith for almost any new system. You get most of microservices' design discipline — bounded contexts, owned data, explicit contracts — with one deployable, one DB, no distributed-systems tax. Extract a service only when forced: a specific subdomain needs independent scaling, a separate team needs independent release cadence, or an operational/availability boundary demands isolation. Microservices are a deployment-time tax that buys autonomy and isolation; pay it only when the value is real, and never to imitate big-tech architecture.**

questions.question: What are the trade-offs between Shared Database and Database per Service in microservices?
questions.title: Shared Database vs Database per Service
questions.direct_answer: **Database per service** is the canonical microservices pattern: each service owns its data exclusively; other services access it only via the service's API. This gives **independent schema evolution, technology choice per workload, and clean failure isolation** — at the cost of **distributed transactions, eventual consistency, and harder cross-service queries**. **Shared database** removes those costs but creates **invisible coupling**: a schema change in one service breaks others; one slow query can lock tables that another service depends on. Use shared DB only as a **transitional state** during a monolith → microservices migration, never as a long-term target.

interviewer_intent.testing: Coupling implications of shared schema, why DB-per-service is the canonical pattern, and how to handle the resulting distributed-data problems (sagas, CQRS, events).
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Sharing tables across services 'just for joins', or treating shared DB as a permanent compromise.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss the spectrum (shared DB, shared schema with per-service tables, shared instance with per-service schemas, separate instances), and how event-driven architecture replaces cross-service joins.

sections.title: The Two Extremes
sections.content:
**Shared Database:** all services connect to the same DB, often share tables.
- Cross-service joins via SQL.
- One team's schema migration affects all services.
- One service's badly indexed query degrades everyone.
- Easy to start, hard to evolve.

**Database per Service:** each service has its own DB instance / schema, accessible only via that service's API.
- No cross-service joins; data composition happens in the application layer or via materialized read models.
- Each service can pick the best DB for its workload (Postgres, Mongo, Cassandra, Elasticsearch).
- Schema changes are local; deployment is independent.
- Distributed transactions need sagas and compensations.

sections.title: Architecture Comparison
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart TB subgraph Shared[Shared DB - tightly coupled] US1[User Service] OS1[Order Service] PS1[Payment Service] DB1[(Shared Postgres
users, orders, payments)] US1 --> DB1 OS1 --> DB1 PS1 --> DB1 OS1 -.JOIN users.-> DB1 PS1 -.JOIN orders.-> DB1 end subgraph PerService[Database per Service] US2[User Service] OS2[Order Service] PS2[Payment Service] UDB[(Postgres
users)] ODB[(Postgres
orders)] PDB[(Postgres
payments)] US2 --> UDB OS2 --> ODB PS2 --> PDB OS2 -.HTTP.-> US2 PS2 -.HTTP/Kafka.-> OS2 end ``` In the shared model, the orange arrows are SQL joins crossing service boundaries — invisible coupling. In DB-per-service, all cross-service data flow is over the network through service APIs.

sections.title: The Spectrum (Not Just Two Options)
sections.content:
Real-world choices sit on a spectrum:

1. **Single shared DB, shared tables** — worst coupling. Avoid except in transitional monoliths.
2. **Single shared DB, per-service tables** — each service writes only its own tables; reads via SQL views or joins. Better, but still shared instance / shared resource pressure.
3. **Single shared instance, per-service schemas** — each service has its own schema (`users_db`, `orders_db`); same Postgres instance. Logically isolated; physically shared. Common compromise.
4. **Separate instances per service** — each service has its own physical DB. Different services can choose different engines. Full isolation.
5. **Separate instances per service + read models** — each service publishes events; other services build local read-only projections for query needs. Best for high-scale systems.

Most mature microservices land at #4 or #5; #3 is a common middle ground for cost-sensitive teams.

sections.title: Trade-Off Matrix
sections.content:
| Aspect | Shared DB | Per-Service DB |
|---|---|---|
| Independent deployment | hard — schema changes affect others | easy |
| Schema evolution | coordinated across teams | per-team |
| Cross-service queries | trivial SQL joins | service calls / read models |
| Transactions | local ACID across services | distributed (Saga) |
| Failure isolation | DB outage = all services down | one service degraded |
| Tech choice per workload | locked to one DB engine | free choice (Postgres, Mongo, Elasticsearch) |
| Resource contention | one slow query slows everyone | per-service capacity |
| Operational complexity | low (one DB) | high (N DBs to back up, monitor, patch) |
| Data consistency | strong | eventual (between services) |
| Cost | lower (one cluster) | higher (N clusters or shared cluster + tooling) |
| Best for | transitional monolith | mature microservices |

sections.title: How to Replace Cross-Service Joins (Per-Service DB)
sections.content:
Without SQL joins across services, you compose data three ways:

**1. API composition (sync orchestration):**
- Order service calls user service for customer details when serving an order page.
- Simple but adds latency; user service must be up.

**2. Local read model / materialized view:**
- User service publishes `UserUpdated` events.
- Order service consumes them and stores `customer_name`, `customer_email` locally (denormalized).
- Eventual consistency, but reads are fast and resilient.
- Best for high-traffic read paths.

**3. CQRS read store:**
- Dedicated read service consumes events from multiple services into Elasticsearch / Postgres.
- Serves complex query needs without coupling write services.
- More infrastructure but very flexible.

Key idea: **events replace joins**. The data still gets joined — just at write time, not query time.

sections.title: Distributed Transactions — Saga Pattern
sections.content:
When a business action spans services (place order = create order + reserve inventory + charge payment), local transactions don't reach across services. The saga pattern coordinates a sequence of local transactions with compensating actions on failure.

```
1. Create order (pending)             [order-svc]
2. Reserve inventory                   [inventory-svc]
3. Charge payment                      [payment-svc]
4. Mark order confirmed                [order-svc]

If step 3 fails:
→ Compensate: release inventory  [inventory-svc]
→ Compensate: cancel order       [order-svc]
```

Two flavors:
- **Choreography:** services react to events from other services.
- **Orchestration:** central saga orchestrator commands each step.

Sagas are correct but require explicit failure planning; you trade ACID for eventual consistency + compensations.

sections.title: When to Use Shared DB (Honestly)
sections.content:
Shared DB isn't always wrong, but it should be a conscious, time-bounded choice:

**Acceptable:**
- **Monolith → microservices migration.** Extract one service at a time, share DB temporarily; migrate data ownership later.
- **Read-only reporting** across multiple services using a read replica or data warehouse — read model, not shared write.
- **Tiny org / single team** owning all services; team coordination cost is low.

**Unacceptable long-term:**
- Production system with multiple teams owning different services on shared write tables.
- Any setup where one team's deploy is blocked by another team's schema migration.

If you find yourself in the unacceptable case, plan extraction: identify each service's tables, give them their own schema first, then their own DB instance.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **'Just join across schemas' in a per-service-schema setup.** Defeats the isolation benefit; treat each schema as if it lived in a different cluster.
- **One team modifying another team's tables.** Even with per-service tables, if other services write to your tables, you don't own them.
- **Sharing the DB but pretending it's per-service.** Lockless inserts in one service still cause hot blocks in another.
- **No data ownership matrix.** Document which service owns which data; otherwise the boundary erodes silently.
- **Cross-service synchronous calls everywhere.** Composes latency and failure; prefer events + local read models for high-traffic reads.
- **Pretending eventual consistency away.** Build the UX assuming a brief lag (e.g., 'your order is being processed' instead of immediate confirm).

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Per-service DB** is the canonical microservices pattern — enables autonomy, independent scaling, tech choice per workload.
- **Shared DB** creates invisible coupling: schema changes ripple, one slow query affects everyone.
- **Spectrum exists:** shared tables → per-service tables → per-service schema → per-service instance → + read models. Mature systems land near the right.
- **Replace joins with events:** local read models, CQRS read stores, API composition.
- **Distributed transactions = sagas + compensations,** not 2PC.
- **Eventual consistency is the norm** between services.
- **Shared DB acceptable only as transitional state** during migration.
- **Document data ownership** explicitly to prevent silent boundary erosion.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**The two extremes**

Shared DB: all services connect to the same DB, often share tables. Cross-service joins via SQL. One team's schema migration affects all. One service's slow query degrades everyone. Easy to start, hard to evolve.

Database per service: each service has its own DB instance/schema, accessible only via the service's API. No cross-service joins. Each service picks the best DB for its workload. Schema changes local. Deployment independent. Distributed transactions need sagas.

**The spectrum**

1. Single shared DB, shared tables — worst coupling, avoid
2. Shared DB, per-service tables — better, still shared instance
3. Shared instance, per-service schemas — logically isolated, physically shared. Common compromise
4. Separate instances per service — different engines per service if needed
5. Separate instances + read models — services publish events, others build local projections. Best for scale

Mature microservices land at 4 or 5.

**Trade-off matrix**

Independent deployment: hard / easy
Schema evolution: coordinated / per-team
Cross-service queries: SQL joins / service calls + read models
Transactions: local ACID / Saga
Failure isolation: DB out = all down / one service degraded
Tech choice: locked / free per workload
Resource contention: one slow query slows all / per-service capacity
Operational complexity: low / high (N DBs)
Consistency: strong / eventual between services

**How to replace cross-service joins**

1. API composition: order service calls user service when serving an order page. Simple but latency cost and synchronous coupling.
2. Local read model: user service publishes UserUpdated events; order service stores customer name/email locally, denormalized. Eventually consistent, fast and resilient. Best for high-traffic reads.
3. CQRS read store: dedicated read service consumes events from multiple services into Elasticsearch. Flexible but more infrastructure.

Events replace joins. Data still gets joined — at write time, not query time.

**Distributed transactions — sagas**

Place order = create order + reserve inventory + charge payment. Local transactions don't reach across services.

Saga: sequence of local transactions with compensating actions on failure. If charge fails: release inventory, cancel order.

Choreography (services react to events) or orchestration (central saga commands each step).

Correct but requires explicit failure planning. Trade ACID for eventual consistency + compensations.

**When shared DB is honest**

Acceptable:
- Monolith → microservices migration: extract one service at a time, share DB temporarily, migrate data ownership later
- Read-only reporting via replica or warehouse — read model, not shared write
- Tiny org / single team owning all services

Unacceptable long-term:
- Multiple teams owning different services on shared write tables
- One team's deploy blocked by another team's schema migration

If in the unacceptable case: identify each service's tables, give them their own schema, then their own instance.

**Common mistakes**

- 'Just join across schemas' — defeats isolation
- One team modifying another team's tables
- Sharing DB but pretending it's per-service
- No data ownership matrix — boundary erodes silently
- Synchronous cross-service calls everywhere — composes latency and failure
- Pretending eventual consistency away — build UX assuming brief lag

**Recommendation**

**Default to database per service for new microservices: own your data, expose only an API, never let another service touch your tables. Replace cross-service joins with local read models populated by events; use sagas for distributed transactions. Shared DB is acceptable only as a transitional state during a monolith decomposition — with a documented plan to split. The spectrum (shared schema → per-service schema → per-service instance) lets you stage the move; aim to land at separate instances + event-driven read models for any system that's expected to live more than a year.**

questions.question: Explain the Strangler Fig Pattern — Incrementally Migrating from Monolith to Microservices.
questions.title: Strangler Fig Pattern — Incrementally Migrating from Monolith to Microservices
questions.direct_answer: The **Strangler Fig pattern** migrates a legacy monolith to a new system **incrementally** by routing specific functionality to new services through a **facade (proxy/gateway)**, while the rest still hits the monolith. Over time, more functionality moves to new services until the monolith is 'strangled' (replaced) without ever a big-bang rewrite. Named after the strangler fig vine that grows around a tree and eventually replaces it. Use it when a full rewrite is too risky, when you need continuous delivery during migration, and when the monolith has clear seams to extract along.

interviewer_intent.testing: Why incremental migration beats big-bang rewrites, the role of the facade/proxy, how to handle data ownership during migration, and the practical sequence of steps.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Routing reads to new service while writes still go to monolith without a sync mechanism (data drift), or extracting the easy/wrong things first instead of the highest-value ones.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Discuss data ownership migration (dual writes, CDC, event sourcing for backfill), how to choose what to extract first (cost, risk, dependency analysis), and metrics to track migration progress.

sections.title: The Idea
sections.content:
Martin Fowler popularized the Strangler Fig pattern (named after the tropical vine that grows around a host tree, eventually replacing it). The core idea: **never rewrite a working system in one big bang**.

Big-bang rewrites fail because:
- Underestimated scope (the monolith encodes years of edge cases nobody documented).
- Two parallel systems must be maintained — features keep shipping in the old one.
- The cutover is high-risk; rollback often impossible.
- Business value pauses during the rewrite.

**Strangler Fig:** route specific URLs / functions to a new service via a facade; everything else keeps hitting the monolith. Migrate one piece at a time, verify, repeat. The monolith shrinks; the new system grows; eventually the monolith disappears.

sections.title: The Facade — Heart of the Pattern
sections.content:
```mermaid flowchart LR Client([Client]) Facade[Facade / API Gateway
routes by URL/path] NewSvc[New Microservice
orders v2] Monolith[Legacy Monolith
everything else] NewDB[(New Service DB)] LegacyDB[(Legacy DB)] Client --> Facade Facade -->|/api/orders/*| NewSvc Facade -->|/api/users/*
/api/products/*
etc| Monolith NewSvc --> NewDB Monolith --> LegacyDB ``` - **Facade** sits in front of the monolith — typically an API gateway, reverse proxy (NGINX, Envoy), or thin Java service. - Routes requests by URL/path/header to either the new service or the legacy monolith. - Clients see one URL (`api.company.com`) regardless of where the work happens. - Migration is a routing change, not a client change. Without the facade, every client would need to know which URLs go where — unmanageable.

sections.title: The Migration Sequence
sections.content:
Typical step-by-step migration of one piece of functionality:

1. **Identify a slice.** Pick a single bounded capability — e.g., order management. Should be cohesive, with clear inputs/outputs, and limited cross-references in the monolith.
2. **Add the facade** in front of the monolith. All traffic still routes to the monolith — no behavioral change yet.
3. **Build the new service** with its own DB and the same external contract as the monolith's old endpoints.
4. **Sync data** — backfill the new DB from the monolith's tables, then keep them in sync (dual writes, CDC, or events).
5. **Shadow traffic** — facade sends a copy of real requests to the new service, compares responses with the monolith, doesn't return new service results to clients yet. Catches regressions safely.
6. **Canary cutover** — facade routes 1% → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100% of orders traffic to the new service.
7. **Decommission monolith code** for that capability — delete the now-unused order classes from the monolith. The strangler has consumed that part of the host.
8. **Decommission shared DB tables** once the monolith no longer reads/writes them.

Repeat for the next slice. Over months to years, the monolith shrinks to nothing.

sections.title: Data Ownership — The Hardest Part
sections.content:
Routing requests is easy; moving data ownership is the hard part. Three common strategies:

**Dual writes:**
- During migration, both monolith and new service write to their respective DBs.
- Facade writes to both (or new service writes through to monolith).
- Risk: writes can succeed in one and fail in the other — partial state. Need reconciliation jobs.

**Change Data Capture (CDC):**
- Use Debezium / Maxwell to stream changes from monolith DB to new service.
- New service builds its DB from the stream.
- During migration, monolith remains the source of truth; new service is a follower.
- After cutover, reverse the direction or stop the stream and let the new service take over writes.

**Event-sourcing backfill:**
- If monolith already publishes domain events, replay them to populate the new service's DB.
- Cleanest, but rare — most monoliths don't emit events.

**Cutover moment:** at some point, the new service must become the source of truth for that data. Before: monolith owns; sync flows monolith → new. After: new service owns; if monolith still needs the data, sync flows reverse direction. This switch is the riskiest moment — plan rollback carefully.

sections.title: How to Pick What to Extract First
sections.content:
Wrong choices can sink the project. Score each candidate slice on:

**Pull (reasons to extract):**
- High change frequency — currently slowed down by monolith deploys.
- Different scaling profile — needs more capacity than the rest.
- Different language/runtime fit — better in Python/Go than the monolith's stack.
- New team or product line wants independent ownership.
- Compliance / security isolation needs.

**Push (reasons it's safe to extract):**
- Few or unidirectional dependencies on/from the rest of the monolith.
- Clear bounded context (DDD analysis helps).
- Already has its own tables.
- Simple data ownership (no shared writes from elsewhere).

**Avoid first:**
- Highly entangled core (auth, billing in the middle of everything) — do these last.
- Tiny pieces with no obvious value — the migration tax overwhelms the benefit.

**Common first picks:** notifications, search, analytics-style read models, image/file handling — typically have clean boundaries and read-mostly workloads.

sections.title: Strangler Fig vs Big Bang Rewrite
sections.content:
| Aspect | Big Bang Rewrite | Strangler Fig |
|---|---|---|
| Risk profile | All-or-nothing at cutover | Incremental; rollback per slice |
| Time to first value | 12-36 months | weeks (per slice) |
| Feature velocity during migration | frozen or duplicated | continuous in the running system |
| Surprise cost | high (edge cases discovered late) | spread out, encountered piece by piece |
| Coordination cost | one massive cutover | many small ones |
| Likelihood of completion | low — most rewrites get cancelled | high — early wins build momentum |
| When OK | tiny systems with no users | almost never |

The industry track record of big-bang rewrites is dismal; strangler fig is the responsible default for any non-trivial system.

sections.title: Common Mistakes
sections.content:
- **Reads to new service, writes to monolith, no sync.** Data drifts — reads return stale data. Always sync (CDC or dual writes) before splitting reads/writes.
- **No facade.** Routing logic in clients = clients must redeploy on every migration step.
- **Extracting the easy thing first.** A small notification service moved doesn't move the needle; a high-pain piece does.
- **No clear cutover criteria.** 'When the new service is ready' is vague; define metrics (error rate < X, latency p99 < Y, parity in shadow tests > 99.9%).
- **Skipping shadow traffic.** First production cutover finds the bugs that staging missed.
- **No deprecation plan.** Old code lingers in the monolith forever, half-used.
- **Rewriting business logic during extraction.** Rule: extract first (preserve behavior), then improve. Don't conflate the two.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Strangler Fig = incremental replacement** of a monolith via a facade.
- **Facade routes by URL/path** to either the new service or the monolith — invisible to clients.
- **Migration sequence:** identify slice → facade in place → build new service → sync data → shadow traffic → canary cutover → decommission old code.
- **Data sync** via dual writes, CDC, or event replay; cutover moment is the riskiest.
- **Pick slices wisely:** pull (change rate, scaling, ownership) + push (low coupling, clear boundaries).
- **Beats big-bang rewrites** by orders of magnitude in success rate.
- **Continuous delivery during migration** is preserved.
- **Don't refactor business logic during extraction** — preserve behavior first, improve later.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
**The idea**

Martin Fowler, named after the strangler fig vine that grows around a host tree and eventually replaces it. Core: never rewrite a working system in one big bang.

Big-bang rewrites fail because: scope underestimated, parallel systems must be maintained, cutover high-risk with no rollback, business value pauses during the rewrite.

Strangler fig: route specific URLs to a new service via a facade; rest still hits the monolith. Migrate one piece at a time. Monolith shrinks, new system grows, eventually monolith disappears.

**The facade — heart of the pattern**

API gateway / reverse proxy / thin Java service in front of the monolith. Routes requests by URL/path/header to either the new service or the legacy monolith.

Clients see one URL regardless of where work happens. Migration is a routing change, not a client change. Without the facade, every client would need to know which URLs go where — unmanageable.

**Migration sequence per slice**

1. Identify a slice — single bounded capability, cohesive, clear inputs/outputs, limited cross-references
2. Add the facade — all traffic still routes to monolith, no behavioral change yet
3. Build the new service with its own DB and the same external contract as the monolith's endpoints
4. Sync data — backfill new DB from monolith tables, keep in sync (dual writes / CDC / events)
5. Shadow traffic — facade sends copies of real requests to new service, compares responses, doesn't return new results yet. Catches regressions safely
6. Canary cutover — 1% → 5% → 25% → 50% → 100%
7. Decommission monolith code for that capability
8. Decommission shared DB tables once monolith no longer needs them

Repeat for next slice. Months to years; monolith shrinks to nothing.

**Data ownership — the hardest part**

Dual writes: both write to their DBs. Facade or new service writes through to monolith. Risk: partial-write inconsistency; need reconciliation jobs.

CDC (Debezium/Maxwell): stream changes from monolith DB to new service. Monolith remains source of truth during migration. After cutover, reverse direction.

Event-sourcing backfill: if monolith publishes events, replay to populate new DB. Cleanest, rare.

Cutover moment: new service becomes source of truth. Before: monolith owns. After: new service owns. Riskiest moment; plan rollback carefully.

**How to pick what to extract first**

Pull (reasons to extract): high change frequency, different scaling profile, different language/runtime, new team wants ownership, compliance isolation.

Push (reasons it's safe): few/unidirectional dependencies, clear bounded context (DDD), already has own tables, simple data ownership.

Avoid first: highly entangled core (auth, billing) — do last. Tiny pieces with no value — migration tax overwhelms benefit.

Common first picks: notifications, search, analytics read models, image/file handling — clean boundaries, read-mostly.

**Strangler vs big bang**

Risk: all-or-nothing at cutover vs incremental rollback per slice
Time to first value: 12-36 months vs weeks per slice
Feature velocity: frozen or duplicated vs continuous
Surprise cost: late and huge vs spread out
Likelihood of completion: low vs high

Big-bang rewrites have dismal industry track record. Strangler fig is the responsible default.

**Common mistakes**

- Reads to new service, writes to monolith, no sync — data drifts
- No facade — routing in clients, redeploy on every step
- Extracting easy things first — doesn't move the needle
- No cutover criteria — 'when ready' is vague; define metrics (error rate, latency p99, shadow parity)
- Skipping shadow traffic — first production cutover finds bugs
- No deprecation plan — old code lingers half-used
- Rewriting business logic during extraction — extract first, improve later

**Recommendation**

**Use the strangler fig pattern for any non-trivial monolith → microservices migration. Put a facade in front, identify a high-value, low-coupling slice (DDD analysis helps), build a new service with the same external contract, sync data via CDC or dual writes, shadow traffic, canary cutover, decommission old code. Pick slices by pull (need for autonomy/scale) and push (low coupling). Never rewrite business logic during extraction — preserve behavior first, improve in a follow-up. Track migration progress with concrete metrics (% traffic on new service, lines of dead monolith code, services with own DB). Big-bang rewrites should be banned by default; strangler fig is the responsible alternative.**
